p1.key: Z = 15 (P) is [Ne]3s23p3: by Hund's rule the three 3p electrons occupy separate orbitals, giving 3 unpaired electrons. Z = 13 has 1, Z = 14 has 2 and Z = 16 has 2.
Emission lines come from electrons falling from higher to lower levels. The lines converge at high frequency because the energy levels get closer together as energy increases.
The big jump comes between the 2nd (1064) and 3rd (4210) ionization energies, so there are two outer electrons. The element is in group 2, the same group as Be.
Energy is released when an electron falls to a lower level (C or D). Levels get closer together as n increases, so the fall from level 2 to level 1 releases far more energy than the fall from 6 to 3.

Chromium is an exception: [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> (B), because a half-filled 3d sublevel is more stable. The markscheme also accepted A (3d<sup>4</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>), the configuration the Aufbau order predicts.
p1.flag: ms accepted A or B; B is the correct ground state

p1.key: By Hund's rule the 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals before pairing: 2p<sup>2</sup> has 2 unpaired, 2p<sup>3</sup> has 3 and 2p<sup>4</sup> has 2 unpaired electrons. All three have unpaired electrons.

The species has 25 electrons, [Ar]3d<sup>7</sup>. Co (27 e⁻) loses its two 4s electrons to give Co<sup>2+</sup> = [Ar]3d<sup>7</sup>. Fe<sup>3+</sup> would be 3d<sup>5</sup>; atoms Co and Mn would have 4s electrons.

Fe [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> has four unpaired d electrons; Cu [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> has one unpaired 4s electron; Zn [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> has all its electrons paired.
Each line comes from an electron falling between two energy levels, with ΔE = hf. The spacing (frequencies) of the lines therefore reveals the energy levels in the atom.
X3+ has 18 + 4 = 22 electrons, so the neutral atom has 22 + 3 = 25 electrons: Z = 25 (manganese, [Ar]3d54s2).

For 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup> (Be), the first two electrons come from the 2s outer shell, but the third must come from the 1s shell, much closer to the nucleus with very little shielding, causing a big jump.
The largest energy drops are transitions to n = 1 (Lyman series), which lie in the ultraviolet. Lines converge at higher energy, emission is from high to low levels, and visible lines end at n = 2.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Ge is [Ar]3d104s24p2. Filled 2p (3 orbitals) + filled 3p (3) + the two 4p electrons in separate orbitals by Hund's rule (2) = 8 occupied p orbitals.
Xe is [Kr]4d105s25p6, and [Kr] contains 3d10. So the d orbitals hold 10 (3d) + 10 (4d) = 20 electrons.
The third ionization energy removes one electron from each 2+ gaseous ion: M<sup>2+</sup>(g) → M<sup>3+</sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup>. C is the sum of the first three IEs.
Emission lines arise when excited electrons fall from higher to lower energy levels, releasing the energy difference as photons of specific frequency.
A large atomic radius and many occupied levels (more shielding) put the outer electron far from the nucleus and weakly held, so the IE is low. A high nuclear charge would raise the IE.
Within a main energy level the sub-levels rise in energy s < p < d < f. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons, level 4 can hold 2n<sup>2</sup> = 32, and f-filling starts at the lanthanides, not Y.
Sn is [Kr]4d105s25p2, so electrons occupy 5 main levels and the outer (fifth) level holds 2 + 2 = 4 electrons (Sn is in group 14).
Fe is [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>. To form Fe<sup>3+</sup> ([Ar]3d<sup>5</sup>), the two 4s electrons are lost first, then one 3d electron.
Valence electrons are those in the outermost (highest) main energy level; they are the electrons involved in bonding.
I: 1s² 2s²2p⁶ 3s²3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s²4p⁶ 4d¹⁰ 5s²5p⁵. p electrons = 6 + 6 + 6 + 5 = 23. Option B (7) counts only valence electrons.
X²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁹ has 18 + 9 = 27 electrons, so the neutral atom has 29 electrons ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹): atomic number 29 (copper). Option A forgets the two removed electrons.
Lines form when electrons fall from higher to lower levels (III), and transitions ending at n = 1 (e.g. 2 → 1) emit UV (Lyman series) (II). The lines converge at higher energy, so I is wrong.
The n = 3 level has 3s (1), 3p (3) and 3d (5) orbitals: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 (n² orbitals). Option B counts only the d orbitals.
Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; Co²⁺ loses the 4s electrons first: [Ar] 3d⁷. Five d orbitals hold 7 electrons by Hund's rule: 5 up, 2 paired, leaving 3 unpaired.
The sharp drop from 2080 to 494 kJ mol⁻¹ shows a new shell starting: a noble gas followed by an alkali metal. So the elements are F (1680), Ne (2080) and Na (494).
Hydrogen emission lines get closer together (converge) at higher energy, i.e. higher frequency and shorter wavelength. B and C describe convergence at the wrong end.

Each successive electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion, so successive ionization energies always increase (IE4 > IE3). First IEs generally increase across period 3, and the second IE removes one electron from a 1+ ion.
Ca²⁺ has 20 − 2 = 18 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, the same as an Ar atom. Al³⁺ has 10 electrons, Br⁻ 36 and K 19.

E and M are the peaks before the big drops, so they are noble gases (I true). F and N are group 1, so G and O are group 2, ns2 (II true). B and J come just before a small dip, so they are group 15 with p3, three half-filled p orbitals (III true). D.
Boron is 1s22s22p1, with three outer electrons. The 4th electron must come from the 1s inner shell, much closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so the biggest jump is between the 3rd and 4th IEs.

The lines in the hydrogen spectrum get closer together as energy increases, converging at higher frequency (shorter wavelength), because the energy levels get closer together further from the nucleus. A and C describe convergence the wrong way round.

The graph shows 4 electrons removed relatively easily, then a big jump, then a further group. So there are 4 electrons in the outer shell, with 8 in the next shell (the 5 shown here are from n = 2): group 14, period 3, Si. C has only 2 inner-shell electrons.
The configuration has 28 electrons. Cu (29 electrons, [Ar]3d104s1) loses its 4s electron to form Cu+, [Ar]3d10. Cu2+ is 3d9, Ni2+ 3d8 and Co3+ 3d6.
Fe is [Ar]3d64s2. When it forms ions the 4s electrons are lost first, then one 3d electron: Fe3+ = [Ar]3d5.
Mg (group 2) has two outer electrons, so the big jump comes between the 2nd and 3rd IEs. In B the 3rd IE is far larger than the 2nd. A jumps after the 1st (group 1) and C after the 3rd (group 13).
Vanadium has 23 electrons: after [Ar] the 4s fills (2) then 3d takes the remaining 3, giving …3d<sup>3</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>. An s sublevel can hold only 2 electrons, so A is impossible.
Visible lines in the hydrogen spectrum (Balmer series) come from electrons falling to n = 2, e.g. 3 → 2. Transitions to n = 1 are ultraviolet, and 2 → 3 is absorption, not emission.
The huge jump is between the 1st (420) and 2nd (3600 kJ mol⁻¹) IE: after one electron is removed, the next comes from a full inner shell. One outer electron means group 1.
Within a main energy level the sublevels increase in energy in the order s < p < d < f.
Sublevels fill in order of increasing energy: 5s then 4d then 5p (as in period 5, Rb–Sr, then Y–Cd, then In–Xe).
Cu is an exception: [Ar]4s<sup>1</sup>3d<sup>10</sup> (a full d sublevel is more stable). Ions lose 4s electrons first: Cu⁺ is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> is [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>.
Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength (E = hc/λ). Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength than infrared, so it also has the greater energy.
Sn is [Kr]5s<sup>2</sup>4d<sup>10</sup>5p<sup>2</sup>. Forming Sn<sup>2+</sup> removes the two outermost 5p electrons, leaving …4p<sup>6</sup>5s<sup>2</sup>4d<sup>10</sup> (option B).

P is 2,8,5. Its first 5 electrons come from shell 3, so there is a big jump between the 5th and 6th IE, then another between the 13th and 14th (moving into shell 1). Only graph A shows jumps after 5 and 13. D (jumps after 2 and 10) is reversed.

The hydrogen spectrum is a line spectrum whose lines converge (get closer together) at higher energy, which is shorter wavelength. In B the lines are close together on the left (short λ) and spread out as wavelength increases. D converges the wrong way.
Cu is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>. When it forms Cu<sup>+</sup>, the 4s electron is lost first, giving [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>.
Ni is [Ar]3d<sup>8</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>. Ni<sup>2+</sup> loses the two 4s electrons first, giving [Ar]3d<sup>8</sup>. Cu<sup>2+</sup> is 3d<sup>9</sup>, and atomic Fe and Ni still have 4s electrons.
Te (Z = 52) is [Kr]5s<sup>2</sup>4d<sup>10</sup>5p<sup>4</sup>. Te<sup>2−</sup> gains 2 electrons, which fills the 5p sublevel: [Kr]5s<sup>2</sup>4d<sup>10</sup>5p<sup>6</sup>. A wrongly uses 5d.

W shows transitions down to n = 1, which are the largest energy gaps. These emit ultraviolet radiation (Lyman series). X (to n = 2) is visible, and the smallest X arrow (3→2) is the red line. Y (to n = 3) has the lowest energy (infrared). Downward arrows mean emission, not heating.

Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before pairing. II pairs electrons in one 2p orbital while another is empty, and III has an unpaired electron with opposite spin. I has three parallel singly occupied orbitals, which is correct.
Emission means the electron falls to a lower level (downward arrows B and D). The largest energy gap is n = 5 → n = 1, so B. A is the same gap but upward, i.e. absorption.
The big jump occurs between the 2nd (1450) and 3rd (7740 kJ mol−1) ionization energies, so Z has 2 valence electrons (group 2) and forms Z2+.
Frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength (c = νλ) and E = hν. UV has a shorter wavelength than IR, so it has a higher frequency and higher energy.
First ionization energy is the energy required (endothermic) to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms. C and D describe electron affinity.
Cu is [Ar]3d104s1. Ions lose 4s electrons first, so Cu+ is 1s22s22p63s23p63d10. C is the configuration of the Cu atom.

The IE falls from Be (2s2) to B (2s22p1) because boron's outer electron is in a higher-energy 2p sub-level, which is easier to remove. B's electron is in the second level, not the third (A); the radius decreases across the period (B).
Se (Z = 34) is [Ar]3d104s24p4; Se2− gains 2 electrons to fill the 4p: 1s22s22p63s23p64s23d104p6. C is the neutral atom; A and B wrongly use 4d.

Lines converge at the high-energy end (right), so M is the lowest-energy line: lowest frequency and longest wavelength. Hence M has a longer wavelength than N; A, B and D are the reverse of the truth.
M2O means M forms M+, so M is in group 1 (sodium). The big jump must come after the first ionization energy: 496 → 4563 kJ mol−1 (option A). B is group 2, C is group 13.
Longest wavelength means smallest energy gap. Energy levels get closer at higher n, so n = 3 → n = 2 releases the least energy. B (n = 1 → 2) is an absorption, not an emission.
Only A and C are emissions (downward arrows); B and D are absorptions. The n = 4 → n = 2 gap (C) is much smaller than n = 2 → n = 1 (A), so C emits the lowest energy and longest wavelength.
The big jump comes after the 6th electron, so there are 6 outer electrons (group 16). At least 10 electrons can be removed, so it must have more than 8 electrons: sulfur (O has only 8).

[Ar]4s<sup>1</sup>3d<sup>5</sup> is chromium, a transition metal (half-filled 3d is more stable than 4s<sup>2</sup>3d<sup>4</sup>). A is K and C is Ge (main group); [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup> is not a ground-state atom configuration (it is Cu<sup>2+</sup>).
Red light has lower energy and lower frequency than blue, so I and III are true. The lines converge at the high-energy, shorter wavelength end, so II is false.
Ionization from the ground state means an electron being promoted from n = 1 to n = ∞ (upward arrow A). B is the reverse (emission) and C starts from n = 2, not the ground state.

Only downward transitions (A and D) emit light. Longest wavelength means lowest energy, and the n = 5 → n = 3 drop (A) is much smaller than n = 3 → n = 1 (D), because energy levels converge at higher n. B and C are absorptions.

X is the highest point just before a huge drop, so X is a noble gas (group 18) and the next element starts a new shell (group 1). Counting on from there, Y is in group 15 (the half-filled p3 element before the group 16 dip), not group 3 or 10.

The lines get closer together (converge) at higher frequency, and transitions down to n = 2 give the visible (Balmer) series. Emission lines come from electrons falling from higher to lower levels, so III is wrong.

X has a huge jump between the 1st and 2nd IE, so it has one outer electron: Li. Z has no big jump over its first three IEs, so it has more than three valence electrons and cannot be Li or Be: C (2s22p2).

Mg+ (…3s1) loses an outer 3s electron from a singly charged ion. Na+ would lose a 2p electron from a full inner shell, while Al2+ and C3+ carry a higher positive charge holding the electron more strongly. So Mg+ needs the least energy.
Chromium is an exception: a half-filled 3d sublevel is more stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d, giving [Ar]4s13d5 rather than the predicted 4s23d4.
The big jump comes between the 6th and 7th ionization energies, so the element has 6 valence electrons (group 16), and the 7th electron comes from an inner shell. Among the options that is sulfur.
Fe is [Ar]4s23d6. When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are removed first, giving Fe2+ = [Ar]3d6.

Energy levels get closer together as n increases, so the smallest gap among these transitions is n = 4 → n = 3, which emits the least energy (in the infrared). Transitions to n = 1 emit the most energy (UV).
An s orbital is spherical, shown as the circle in A. The dumbbell shapes are p orbitals, and B and D show orbitals overlapping, not a single s orbital.

IE rises across period 2 but with two dips: B is lower than Be (its 2p electron is higher in energy than 2s) and O is lower than N (repulsion between paired electrons in a 2p orbital). Graph C shows both dips; A shows only the first.

The large jump comes between the 6th and 7th ionization energies (≈9000 → ≈16 000 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>): the 7th electron is removed from an inner shell. Six valence electrons → group 16 (labelled “6” in old group numbering).
p1.flag: options use old group numbering (6 = group 16)

p1.key: 2s holds two electrons with opposite spins (Pauli); the two 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule). C and D break the Pauli principle; B has opposed spins in 2p.
The big jump comes between the 3rd and 4th ionization energies (≈2700 → ≈11 600 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>), so there are 3 valence electrons: aluminium (group 13).
